saints.dates: Byzantine period; exact chronology not established here

summary.text: Symeon, rendered Simeon on the cited page, is remembered as a monk and spiritual writer associated with Constantinople. The life distinguishes him from his elder Simeon the Pious and identifies Nicetas Stethatos as his biographer. It also notes the transfer of his feast from March 12 to October 12 because of Lent. The displayed date follows this source entry rather than overriding parish practice.

blocks.text: Benedict XVI’s biographical address describes Symeon’s education in Constantinople and his turn from a projected public career toward monastic life. It identifies Symeon the Pious as his spiritual guide and connects his reading of ascetical authors with the experience later described in his writings. This is a modern Roman Catholic account of an Eastern saint, used here for identified biographical context, not as an Orthodox jurisdictional pronouncement.

blocks.text: The biographical address distinguishes the Studite monastery, his move to Saint Mamas, and his eventual leadership there. It connects difficulties at the Studion with his unusual devotion to his elder and his mystical experiences. It also records rehabilitation by Patriarch Sergius II after exile, and places much of his later writing at Saint Marina. These details give the institutional setting for a life remembered principally through his teachings and his disciple’s biography.

blocks.text: At Saint Mamas, Symeon’s reform met resistance and an attack by some monks; the Life says he sought leniency for them. He later resigned the abbacy to write. Conflict with ecclesiastical authorities led to banishment across the Bosphorus and continued monastic life.

blocks.text: GOARCH places Symeon with John the Evangelist and Gregory among the saints called Theologian. It associates this title with his teaching and life; it is not an academic degree.

blocks.text: The address identifies Nicetas Stethatos as the best-known disciple who preserved Symeon’s writings and compiled his posthumous Life. It also distinguishes catecheses, treatises, and hymns rather than treating every text circulated under his name as the same work. The disciple’s relationship to the saint matters when reading that Life as an attributed witness.
